articles.body:
'A Yalta format will not bring about peace,' Merz warns

Merz is the first to speak.

He says the leaders want “a peace for Ukraine that is both just and lasting,” with “more, not less, security for Europe and the world.”

“We will continue to support Kyiv for as long as is necessary. Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A “Yalta-style” format will not bring about peace.”

He says that as a gift he gave each of the guests a piece of the Berlin Wall, as an example of “what the Yalta arrangement represented for Berlin.”

“You may recall that in 1987, President Reagan stood here in Berlin and said: ‘Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!’ Today, we say to President Putin: ‘end the war in Ukraine, and let us work together to find diplomatic solutions.’ We never again want to live in a divided Europe. We want to live in freedom and in peace – together.”

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

European leaders showed a united and defiant front as they repeated their backing for Ukraine “for as long as it takes” at the latest summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, declaring no decisions on Ukraine and Europe can be made without their participation (17:58, 18:06, 18:11).

Their comments appeared to play down the importance of Donald Trump’s summit with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen (16:34), with German chancellor Friedrich Merz saying “a Yalta format will not bring about peace,” in a reference to secretive discussions between superpowers above the heads of those most affected (17:45, 17:50).

European leaders and US peace envoys insisted that some progress has been made in discussions on ending the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine, although they struck a cautious note about Putin’s intentions in the coming months (15:46, 18:38, 18:44).

US envoy Jared Kushner claimed that Russia’s leadership appears to be “comfortable” with the concept of Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine in any postwar settlement (18:29).

Meanwhile, Russia’s Putin struck an uncompromising tone at his press briefing in Shenzhen, vowing “painful” response to Ukraine’s attacks on Kerch bridge and defending his maximalist demands (13:09, 13:34).

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast

Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump,Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China.

Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity?

Here is our latest “Politics Weekly” podcast on this if you want to catch up on today’s events:

Separately, Poland’s Donald Tusk also told reporters on his way back to Poland that Trump’s comments after his meeting with Putin and Xi sounded “quite optimistic.”

But Tusk quickly added that Trump’s “faith in Putin’s good will is probably unshakeable,” and he was a bit more sceptical about it.

“It would be good if indeed sooner or later it turned out that Russia is seriously ready to undertake peace talks,” he said.

But he warned:

“I don’t think it’s likely that Russia will sit down at the negotiating table in any serious way before the winter is over.”

'Some grounds for optimism' that talks can progress, Burnham says

The European leaders also get asked about Welt/Politico’s report earlier and the tone of Trump’s comments.

Burnham says that Trump’s comments focused on “horrific” loss of life during the war, saying “he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”

He stresses “nobody is winning this war,” and stresses that in his view there has been “huge progress” in now consensus that “there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room and no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room.”

He says “there is a greater degree of alignment.”

“I would say for the first time in my period as prime minister of the United Kingdom, I see alignment; I see people saying the same thing; I see solidarity across the board in Europe; a strong, united European position.

And that gives some grounds for optimism that there can now be progress. But obviously, there is one person who can determine that more than anybody else, and that is president Putin.”

Witkoff jumps in there to say that Trump has “adamantly supported a peaceful end to this war,” with clear instructions to engage with the coalition of the willing and work in all formats that can be helpful to end the war.

“What I heard from him on the call today was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders who he was meeting with [Xi and Putin], so he made Ukraine, and a peaceful end to this war, a principal part of that trilateral today, and I think he’s to be commended for that.”

Russia 'comfortable' with Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine, Kushner says

Kushner says that the US managed to get Moscow comfortable with the concept that any security agreement for Ukraine would be based on Article 5-type arrangement, like in Nato.

(Not sure the Russians would say the same.)

He says “I know that there’s a lot of, scepticism and disbelief on that concept in Russia, but that’s why it’s important to restart the dialogue between Europe and Russia.”

He says:

“I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article Five like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to. but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that and … we have to make sure it is part of a broader security package.”

Merz gets a question on potential multilateral talks with Ukraine, Russia, Europe and the US, and confirms that’s the plan and adds that finding the right place for it shouldn’t be too difficult.

He also goes back to his Yalta reference earlier, saying Europe was “parcelled up” by powers, and “we will not allow anything like that to happen again.”

Macron says the focus is on safeguarding Europe’s security.

He said that a peace declaration agreed by Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China “does not lead to a reorganisation of the world”.

“Today, if there is one critical factor in Europe’s reorganisation, its security, it is precisely the meeting that took place in Berlin,” he said.

Trump comes away from China talks thinking peace is achievable, Kushner says

US Kushner is up next.

He says the meeting was “very substantive and successful,” and “essential in helping us shape our point of views,” as he confirms that Trump dialled in for parts of the talks.

He pointedly praises Italy’s Meloni, Poland’s Tusk, European Commission’s von der Leyen, Nato’s Rutte, Finnish president and Norwegian PMs, Stubb and Gahr Støre.

He says Europe is “very united, and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine,” which he and Witkoff “relayed to president Trump.”

He says, without revealing details, that Trump came away from the trilateral China meeting thinking “peace is achievable”.

“For us, success in an outcome would be to have a sovereign, secure, prosperous and free Ukraine at the end of the war,” he says.

He says the talks have been making “a lot of progress” on postwar prosperity plan, security guarantees, and a plan to exchange prisoners of war.

On postwar security, he says that “Nato will be a central pillar” of proposals, with the right structures to avoid accidental escalations.

Kushner also says that Russians appear to be “willing to trust” the US suggestion that Europeans need to be included in the process to make sure that whatever agreement is struck will be respected.

The US envoys will be meeting with national security advisers next to agree on the detail of their proposals.

“President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” he insists..

“Our goal is really to end this war and to really help build a durable peace. We are very committed. President Trump, will do whatever it takes to do that. He’s instructed us to commit as much time as possible, and we will continue to do that in full coordination, and unity with our European partners.”

'Not for the aggressor to set out wide raging and unrealistic security demands' Burnham says

UK’s Burnham speaks next.

He says today’s meeting “has put on a huge show of support” for Kyiv, and “the mood was stronger, more united, more determined.”

“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.”

He says the coalition is ready for discussions on European security, but only “if there is a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”

He says the UK’s support for Ukraine will continue for “as long as it takes.”

“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.

And I hope that message is heard very clearly, in Moscow: for as long as it takes.”

“If we want to be credible in peace negotiations, then it is important that Ukraine defends itself and goes into these negotiations in a good position, and Ukraine can only do so if we continue supporting Ukraine.”

He adds:

“Everyone who is here today have to do everything in their power so that Ukraine has everything it needs in order to resist and to defend herself …”

He says that faced with Russia’s maximalist demands, it’s time it is “the right point in time to discuss [Ukraine’s] Nato membership.”

Commenting on the current state of talks, he says Russia “did not submit any concrete and tangible proposals for peace.”

He acknowledges that “the coming weeks will be critical” for Ukraine, and so the coalition gathered at the right moment.

He says there was every attempt made to “make this meeting as concrete as possible.”

He thanks all partners for helping Ukraine and highlights “active efforts to ensure that we stand firm.”

He thanks the EU for its “very substantial” proposed loan of £45bn.

He also highlights some of the priority areas for Ukraine, including the move to stop daily drone attacks (which he confirms hit the Austrian and the Dutch embassies), and deploy more air defence systems.

He also says the next round of talks should include European leaders, and highlights the importance of security guarantees and Ukraine’s future membership in the EU.

articles.summary: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."

articles.body:
Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?

November 19, 2026

The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."

Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.

Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.

The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.

Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.

The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.

While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."

Who gained the most from the meeting?

For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."

Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.

The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."

Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits

The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.

Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.

But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.

Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.

Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.

"The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."

The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."

"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.

But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.

A reluctant host?

China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.

Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.

But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted.

"China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."

Warnings of a 'second Yalta'

Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.

That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.

In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."

But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.

Will there be more such trilaterals?

Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.

Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.

"Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

articles.body:
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.

The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.

It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.

The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.body:
United Arab Emirates

Somalia on Thursday expelled the United Arab Emirates ambassador, accusing the Gulf nation of interfering in its internal affairs, government authorities said.

Somalia and the UAE have faced growing tensions over several issues, including Abu Dhabi's perceived support for Israel's recognition of the breakaway region of Somaliland.

"The Council instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation to recall Somalia’s Ambassador to the UAE... and to notify the UAE Ambassador to Somalia to leave the country within 72 hours," Somalia's Information Minister Abdulfatah Qasim said. The expulsion followed a cabinet meeting at which the UAE was accused of "blatant aggression against Somalia".

"The Somali government is taking a series of measures... to defend the country against UAE actions targeting its sovereignty, territorial integrity, national unity, internal security and independence," Qasim said.

In January, Somalia cancelled all agreements with the UAE in the wake of Israel's recognition of Somaliland, and after the UAE allegedly helped a Yemeni separatist leader escape by boat and plane through Somali ports without asking the government's permission.

The UAE built and operates a large deep-water port and military base at Berbera in Somaliland and two others at Bosaso and Kismayo in other parts of Somalia.

Although the Somali government said it would no longer be permitted to operate these ports, Somalia is deeply fragmented and the federal government has practically no control over the semi-autonomous states where the ports are located.

articles.body:
E' morto Corrado Augias, giornalista, scrittore, conduttore e autore televisivo. Nato a Roma il 26 gennaio 1935, aveva 91 anni.

Scrittore, giornalista, conduttore televisivo, drammaturgo, politico, Augias è stato soprattutto un uomo di cultura. Un intellettuale vecchio stampo, di quelli che non esistono più, e grande divulgatore culturale.

La sua passione profonda per la letteratura, la musica, la storia, la conoscenza della società in cui viviamo, il suo garbo nei modi e nello stile, la sua autoironia e straordinaria memoria lo hanno reso, a 91 anni, un grande punto di riferimento in programmi di successo come la Torre di Babele che ha condotto dal 2023 fino ai suoi ultimi giorni su La7.

"Ho appreso con profonda tristezza la notizia della scomparsa di Corrado Augias e conservo il ricordo di un giornalista libero e di uno scrittore di grande finezza, che ha attraversato decenni di vita italiana ed europea, con spirito critico, misura e inesauribile curiosità", ha scritto in una nota il presidente della Repubblica, Sergio Mattarella. "Con i suoi libri, i suoi articoli, le sue rubriche e presenze televisive - ricorda il capo dello Stato - ha svolto una preziosa opera di trasmissione di cultura e di valori di democrazia. Ha avvicinato generazioni di cittadini alla letteratura, alla storia, alla musica, alla vita sociale senza mai rinunciare al rigore della ricerca, all'esercizio del dubbio, alla pratica del dialogo e al rispetto per le opinioni altrui. La sua cultura, la sua passione civile, radicata profondamente nei valori della Costituzione, il suo garbo - conclude - resteranno un riferimento per quanti lo hanno conosciuto e stimato. Esprimo alla Signora Augias, a sua figlia Natalia, ai suoi amici e collaboratori il cordoglio più sentito e la vicinanza nel loro dolore a nome della Repubblica e mio personale".

La camera ardente di Corrado Augias sarà allestita sabato 21 novembre nella Sala della Protomoteca in Campidoglio. L'ultimo saluto sarà possibile dalle ore 10 alle ore 18. L'ingresso in Protomoteca per il pubblico avverrà dalla scalinata del Vignola.

Il cordoglio della Rai

Un acuto, e arguto, osservatore del nostro tempo e uno dei volti simbolo, per decenni, della Rai. Così l'amministratore delegato Rai, Giampaolo Rossi, il Cda e l'intera azienda ricordano Corrado Augias, scomparso oggi, e si stringono affettuosamente ai suoi familiari. Dai tempi del Tg1, negli anni '60, lo sguardo di Augias ha spaziato dalla cronaca alla cultura, con un linguaggio tanto appassionato e rigoroso quanto coinvolgente e capace di parlare a tutti i pubblici. Nella storia della Rai restano programmi preziosi come il suo Telefono Giallo, Quante Storie, Città segrete, senza dimenticare le incursioni nel mondo dei libri in Babele e in quelle nella musica classica con La gioia della musica, insieme all'Orchestra Rai. A lui, va il pensiero riconoscente di tutta l'azienda, con la profonda consapevolezza che quanto Augias ha dato al Servizio Pubblico resta un patrimonio comune, al quale continuare a ispirarsi.

Salerno (La7): 'Ciao Corrado ti ricorderemo come abbiamo deciso insieme'

"Ciao Corrado, grazie di tutto quello che ci hai dato, insegnato. Grazie del lavoro fatto assieme. Tutta @La7tv si stringe a Natalia, ai tuoi cari nipoti e alle persone che ti hanno voluto bene. Ti ricorderemo come abbiamo deciso assieme". Lo scrive il direttore de La7 Andrea Salerno sui social. All'ANSA Salerno spiega come sarà ricordato: "Oggi ricorderemo Corrado in tutti i programmi della Rete. Lunedì, nel suo giorno storico di messa in onda, e come lui voleva, gli dedicheremo la sua ultima "prima serata" con una puntata speciale che abbiamo costruito proprio insieme a lui".

Schlein: 'Ha aiutato la nostra coscienza civile, ci lascia una grande ricchezza di idee'

"La scomparsa di Corrado Augias è una perdita profonda per il giornalismo, la cultura e soprattutto per la coscienza civile del nostro Paese. Ha raccontato la storia e le sue contraddizioni con una straordinaria capacità di parlare, e risvegliare, generazioni diverse e ha portato la cultura nello spazio pubblico, rendendola accessibile senza semplificarla, avvicinando tante persone alle grandi questioni del nostro tempo comprese quelle etiche - così in una nota la segretaria del Partito democratico, Elly Schlein -. Non ha mai avuto paura di confrontarsi in prima persona sui grandi temi che ci attraversano, compresa la morte, mostrandoci quanto la conoscenza e la coscienza siano fondamento di una democrazia viva e consapevole. A ben vedere lascia un vuoto, sì, ma ci lascia anche una grande ricchezza di idee. Alla sua famiglia e ai suoi cari vanno le mie più sentite condoglianze e quelle di tutta la comunità del Partito Democratico".

Conte: 'Augias ci ha insegnato che cultura è indispensabile per essere liberi'

"Con i suoi articoli, i suoi libri, la sua tv ci ha insegnato che la cultura è una chiave indispensabile per essere liberi, interpretare e affrontare le sfide del nostro tempo, aprire le porte su un futuro migliore. Quella di Corrado Augias è una perdita grande per il Paese. Il M5S si stringe in un abbraccio attorno al dolore dei suoi cari", scrive sui social il leader dei 5 stelle, Giuseppe Conte.

articles.title: I film della settimana
articles.summary: Da Fjord di Cristian Mungiu a La ballata del re delle api di Andrew Patterson. Le recensioni della stampa straniera
articles.preview: Con Fjord (Palma d’oro a Cannes 2026) Cristian Mungiu s’interroga: in un paese, o in un continente, possono coesistere persone dai valori profondamente contrastanti? articles.body:
Con Fjord (Palma d’oro a Cannes 2026) Cristian Mungiu s’interroga: in un paese, o in un continente, possono coesistere persone dai valori profondamente contrastanti? Da un lato una frangia progressista che vuole liberarsi dalla tradizione, dall’altro un fronte conservatore che sta sulla difensiva. È possibile trovare un terreno comune? Il regista romeno, che si è ispirato ad alcuni casi di cronaca, rifugge facili risposte preferendo usare gli strumenti del cinema per condividere le sue preoccupazioni e coinvolgere empaticamente lo spettatore nella riflessione. Tutto comincia con l’arrivo in Scandinavia dalla Romania della famiglia Gheorghiu: Mihai (Stan), ingegnere informatico romeno, la moglie Lisbet (Reinsve), infermiera norvegese, e i loro cinque figli di cui uno ancora in fasce. Questa famiglia evangelica, estremamente pia, sembra adattarsi bene al nuovo ambiente finché, nella scuola frequentata dai ragazzi più grandi, alcune segnalazioni fanno scattare l’intervento dei servizi sociali. I bambini sono portati via ai genitori in attesa dei procedimenti civili e penali scattati più o meno automaticamente. Mungiu, sempre attento all’umanità dei personaggi, si concentra su tre livelli sovrapposti. Il primo è all’interno della famiglia, in cui non mancano apparenti contraddizioni. Il secondo è sull’aspro scontro di valori tra la famiglia e le istituzioni, due ambienti che sembrano fare a gara di intransigenza. Infine c’è il fragile legame di solidarietà tra i Gheorghiu e i loro vicini di casa, quello che infonde un po’ di speranza al film.

Boris Bastide, Le Monde

Romania / Norvegia / Svezia / Danimarca / Finlandia / Francia 2026, 146’. In sala

Stati Uniti 2026, 130’. In sala

Se il ritorno sullo schermo di Matthew McConaughey dopo anni di assenza può essere indicativo della strada che l’attore intende seguire da qui in avanti, abbiamo un segnale entusiasmante. La ballata del re delle api è il secondo film di Andrew Patterson dopo The vast of night, sorprendente film di fantascienza rétro e a basso costo. Ambientato in Oklahoma, La ballata del re delle api è un film difficile svincolato dalle convenzioni commerciali in termini di struttura o genere, ed è impossibile da riassumere. È la tenera storia di un uomo che ritrova una giovane donna che aveva avuto in affidamento, un omaggio chiassoso a una comunità rurale, una rappresentazione dell’industria dell’apicoltura e anche un dramma di vendetta. Il film si concentra sempre prima di tutto sulle persone, raccontando una realtà depressa in cui si può scegliere se predare gli altri o cercare di aiutarsi a vicenda. E “l’affetto” che permea il film non viene mai sminuito dalla romanticizzazione. Un film folle, nel senso migliore del termine. Alison Willmore, Vulture

India 2026, 195’. In sala

Film indiano in lingua hindi più costoso della storia e prima parte dell’adattamento del poema epico sanscrito, Ramayana. La nascita di una leggenda è un melodramma massimalista popolato da clan in guerra, elefanti volanti corazzati, ibridi tra uomini e uccelli. Un fantasy un po’ discontinuo ma incredibilmente divertente. Kapoor interpreta un principe virtuoso finito in esilio, ma destinato a un futuro da eroe. Il film acquista slancio ogni volta che entriamo nel regno del dispotico Ravana (Yash, eccellente), un incrocio tra il rave di Sirāt e una sequenza di battaglia tratta da Il signore degli anelli.

Wendi Ide, The Observer

Stati Uniti / Regno Unito 2026, 118’. In sala

Nella non del tutto indegna rivisitazione di Ti West (autore della trilogia X) del Canto di Natale, ci si poteva aspettare un’incursione in qualche spazio inesplorato. Non è così: poco dopo l’inizio, ci ritroviamo pari pari nella storia che il Fantasma del Natale passato racconta da 180 anni, stavolta con uno stile da horror britannico anni settanta. Depp risulta un po’ ingombrante, ma il film, nel complesso si può guardare.

Donald Clarke,The Irish Times

articles.body:
Esta es la primera vez en su historia que el Tribunal Internacional de Justicia considera a un Estado responsable de ese gravísimo delito. La decisión puede repercutir en el caso iniciado por Sudáfrica contra Israel

El Tribunal Internacional de Justicia (TIJ) de la ONU ha concluido este jueves que Myanmar (antes Birmania) ha cometido un genocidio contra la minoría musulmana rohinyá, al considerar por nueve votos a favor frente a seis en contra que el país violó la Convención para la Prevención y la Sanción del Genocidio (1948) al no impedir que sus Fuerzas Armadas masacraran al menos a 10.000 personas, violaran y ejercieran diversos “actos de violencia extrema” sobre adultos y niños rohinyás en 2017. Esta es la primera vez en su historia que el máximo órgano judicial de Naciones Unidas declara responsable de un genocidio a un Estado.

Durante la lectura del fallo del caso iniciado por Gambia en el TIJ contra Myanmar por presunto genocidio contra los rohinyás, el ponente de la sentencia, el presidente del TIJ, Yuji Iwasawa, ha expresado la “plena convicción” del tribunal de que las fuerzas de seguridad de Myanmar mataron a miles de rohinyás, quemaron sistemáticamente sus casas, destruyeron sus pueblos y perpetraron diversas atrocidades. Esas operaciones militares, ejecutadas desde octubre de 2016, han obligado a casi un millón de rohinyás a huir al vecino Bangladés.

Iwasawa ha subrayado que las autoridades de Myanmar actuaron con “la intención de destruir a una parte sustancial” de esa minoría en el norte del estado de Rakáin, en el oeste del país, un elemento fundamental para determinar si se cometió genocidio, según el derecho internacional. Los jueces del tribunal han considerado, por 11 votos a favor y cuatro en contra, que Myanmar no solo no evitó el genocidio de los rohinyás, sino que tampoco ha cumplido con su obligación de castigar a quienes lo cometieron. En la sentencia, el TIJ ordena a Myanmar que investigue a los responsables, indemnice a las víctimas y facilite el regreso de los desplazados.

“El Tribunal considera que las fuerzas de seguridad de Myanmar mataron a miles de civiles rohinyás, perpetraron actos generalizados de violencia sexual, incluidas violaciones, así como actos de violencia extrema contra niños, y atacaron a los rohinyás que huían mientras intentaban escapar en gran número hacia Bangladés”, ha afirmado el ponente. Luego ha indicado que las aldeas donde vivían los miembros de esa minoría fueron destruidas en 2017, antes de que personas ajenas al grupo se instalaran en esas localidades.

Además de los daños físicos causados por toda esta violencia, estos actos tuvieron un “grave impacto en la salud física y mental” de un “número muy significativo” de rohinyás. Myanmar adoptó asimismo medidas destinadas a “impedir” que los miembros de esta comunidad tuvieran descendencia y “ralentizar su tasa de nacimientos”, otra de las condiciones que incluye la Convención para la Prevención y la Sanción del Genocidio para considerar que se cometió ese delito, el más grave que recoge el derecho internacional.

El caso de Israel

La decisión puede tener implicaciones para la interpretación y aplicación de la Convención sobre el genocidio y la lucha contra la impunidad, ahora que el propio TIJ tramita la demanda presentada en 2023 por Sudáfrica contra Israel, en virtud del mismo tratado, por su “conducta genocida” contra la población palestina de Gaza.

“Esta es una victoria histórica para los rohinyás y un hito para la justicia internacional”, declara el abogado estadounidense Reed Brody. Para los rohinyás, que han sufrido décadas de persecución, masacres, violaciones masivas y desplazamientos forzados, “esta sentencia supone una profunda reivindicación”. “Su sufrimiento ha sido finalmente reconocido por el tribunal más alto del mundo”, concluye.

El juez japonés Iwasawa, el presidente del TIJ, ha advertido de que el 1,2% de los cerca de un millón de rohinyá han perecido a causa de la violencia padecida a manos del ejército de Myanmar. La versión oficial del Estado birmano era que se trataba de combatir la insurgencia presente en el seno de las aldeas de esta minoría étnica. Sin embargo, “ello creó una atmósfera de la que se deduce que las fuerzas de seguridad tenían la intención de atacar y matar a la población”, ha afirmado. “Myanmar sabía, o debió saber y prevenir los actos de violencia genocida cometidos contra los rohinyá por las fuerzas armadas”, ha añadido.

El abogado Brody subraya que “al rechazar los argumentos de Myanmar”, en particular “su justificación de las atrocidades como parte de unas ‘supuestas operaciones antiterroristas’, el tribunal también abre la puerta a que se rechacen argumentos similares por parte de Israel, que sostiene que sus operaciones militares en Gaza están dirigidas contra Hamás”, destaca este jurista especializado en derechos humanos y justicia universal. “La existencia de un conflicto armado o de un objetivo de seguridad”, continúa Brody, “no excluye la intención genocida”.

Israel, mientras tanto, guarda silencio. Aunque pueden quedar años para su sentencia, la tesis de que comete un genocidio en Gaza desde 2023 no ha hecho más que ganar peso en distintos ámbitos. La Asociación Internacional de Académicos del Genocidio —la más importante que estudia el tema— ya concluyó en 2025 que las acciones de Israel “cumplen la definición jurídica de genocidio”. Es también la conclusión de la Comisión Independiente de Investigación del Consejo de Derechos Humanos de la ONU y de distintas ONG, tanto internacionales (Amnistía Internacional, Human Rights Watch…) como israelíes, caso de B’tselem o Médicos por los Derechos Humanos.

Para Benjamín Netanyahu, la acusación es “el mundo al revés”. “El Estado de Israel es acusado de genocidio, mientras lucha contra el genocidio [por parte de Hamás]”, aseguró tras la primera audiencia. El primer ministro también ha usado el argumento de que, si su país hubiera querido cometer un genocidio, habría tardado minutos, porque dispone de capacidad militar para el exterminio. Además de la acusación de genocidio contra su país en el Tribunal Internacional de Justicia, el propio Netanyahu está bajo orden de arresto por otro tribunal con sede en La Haya, el Penal Internacional, como sospechoso de crímenes de guerra y contra la humanidad en Gaza en el mismo periodo, informa Antonio Pita.

Intención genocida

Para concluir que se ha perpetrado un genocidio, hay que demostrar la intención genocida. Que se ha querido destruir, en todo o en parte, a un grupo nacional, étnico, racial o religioso en cuanto a tal.

Iwasawa ha desgranado los factores que marcan esa intención en este caso de manera ordenada. Ha subrayado que se ha impedido la cohesión de los rohinyás como grupo a base de evitar que formasen familias o de separar a los menores de su comunidad. Ha recordado que el Ejército de Myanmar “ha deshumanizado” a esta minoría en sus actos y declaraciones, difundidas incluso a través de redes sociales —ha citado expresamente Facebook—. Ha indicado que han sido señalados de manera concreta en las zonas donde vivían, que acabaron siendo destruidas, siendo la población desplazada a la fuerza por las operaciones militares sin que hayan podido regresar a su tierra.

En cuanto a la violencia sexual, ha subrayado: “Las Fuerzas Armadas de Myanmar la han perpetrado de manera sistemática, con violaciones en masa en algunos lugares”, ha dicho Iwasawa. “Es difícil, por otro lado, explicar por qué se mata a niños para llevar a cabo estas operaciones militares contra elementos insurgentes”, ha indicado.

El caso llegó en 2019 al TIJ a instancias de Gambia, un país africano situado a miles de kilómetros de Myanmar y que no está implicado. De mayoría musulmana, Gambia demandó a Myanmar cumpliendo con el mandato de la Convención sobre el genocidio, que obliga a los Estados firmantes a prevenir, perseguir y castigar a los culpables de violarla, ya sea en tiempos de paz o de guerra.

Brody recuerda que Gambia también merece un reconocimiento especial. Dice: “En un momento en que algunas de las mayores potencias del mundo, incluidos Estados Unidos y Rusia, desafían abiertamente el derecho internacional, Gambia, un pequeño país de África occidental sin ningún interés directo en el conflicto, recurrió a la justicia para defender a un pueblo al otro lado del mundo”.

Los rohinyás son una minoría étnica musulmana que ha sufrido marginación en un país de mayoría budista, y llevan generaciones viviendo en el Estado de Rakáin (situado en la costa oeste de la antigua Birmania, en la frontera con Bangladés).

En 1982, Myanmar aprobó una ley que los excluía de la ciudadanía, perdiendo con ello sus derechos y libertades. Entre 2016 y 2017, las fuerzas armadas de Myanmar sometieron a la comunidad a actos de una violencia extrema que obligaron a huir a unos 700.000 de sus miembros. En estos momentos, cerca de un millón está refugiado en Bangladés. En 2019, un informe de la Misión Internacional Independiente de Investigación de la ONU sobre Myanmar concluyó que la violencia desatada constituía “los crímenes más graves del derecho internacional”.

articles.title: “Volarle la cabeza a Sánchez”: la conversación que convenció al PSOE de personarse en la causa contra Núcleo Nacional
articles.summary: Los socialistas creen que el grupo neonazi, cuya dirigente Isabel Peralta amenazó al presidente, pone en riesgo “la paz pública, la dignidad de la persona, la igualdad y el pluralismo político”
articles.preview: Los socialistas creen que el grupo neonazi, cuya dirigente Isabel Peralta amenazó al presidente, pone en riesgo “la paz pública, la dignidad de la persona, la igualdad y el pluralismo político” El PSOE se ha tomado muy en serio las amenazas contra Pedro Sánchez en la causa judicial contra el grupo neonazi Núcleo Nacional, investigado por su presunta participación en delitos de odio, asociación ilícita y tenencia de armas.
articles.body:
Los socialistas creen que el grupo neonazi, cuya dirigente Isabel Peralta amenazó al presidente, pone en riesgo “la paz pública, la dignidad de la persona, la igualdad y el pluralismo político”

El PSOE se ha tomado muy en serio las amenazas contra Pedro Sánchez en la causa judicial contra el grupo neonazi Núcleo Nacional, investigado por su presunta participación en delitos de odio, asociación ilícita y tenencia de armas. La Policía Nacional detuvo a principios de noviembre a 14 miembros de la organización ultraderechista en una operación en la que incautaron armas de fuego y armas blancas. Los socialistas han decidido personarse en la causa después de que la portavoz de Núcleo Nacional, Isabel Peralta, se planteara, según las conversaciones registradas por las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad, la idoneidad de publicar un vídeo en redes en el que reclamara “volarle la cabeza a Pedro Sánchez”.

Aunque finalmente no lo hizo, el PSOE considera que se trata de unas “amenazas” que, “de resultar acreditadas” en la investigación instruida bajo secreto de sumario por el Juzgado de Instrucción número 1 de Gijón, “podrían ser constitutivas de un delito de amenazas del artículo 169 del Código Penal, sin perjuicio de cualquier otra calificación que proceda”, según la petición del PSOE para personarse en el proceso judicial. El citado artículo regula el delito de amenazas graves con hasta cinco años de prisión.

Los servicios jurídicos de Ferraz consideran que el riesgo era tangible. El motivo es que Peralta almacenaba un arsenal con 13 armas largas (entre ellas, 10 fusiles de los modelos M16, R15 y AR-15), tres pistolas y decenas de cajas de munición, según el registro que se realizó en su domicilio de Pinto (Madrid). La Policía Nacional considera que la dirigente de Núcleo Nacional “está dispuesta a sacrificar su vida en defensa de su ideario y ha llegado a insinuar la creación de un movimiento armado”. En las conversaciones registradas por los investigadores, aparecen decenas de referencias al uso de fusiles y pistolas. “Estamos hablando de la intención de asesinar al presidente del Gobierno y secretario general del PSOE por parte de una dirigente de un grupo paramilitar al que se le incautaron decenas de armas”, advierten fuentes de la dirección federal del PSOE para las que “no es una simple provocación”, sino “una amenaza real”.

En su escrito, el PSOE destaca además que Peralta, a la que considera “la cabeza visible” de Núcleo Nacional, “ha verbalizado que ‘qué pena que vaya a dimitir Pedro Sánchez, que no puede jugar a replicar planes americanos’, como clara referencia al asalto del Congreso de los Estados Unidos por parte de los seguidores de Donald Trump después de perder las elecciones de 2020″.

El grupo neonazi desmantelado por la Policía planeaba “un alzamiento” y con ese propósito algunos de sus miembros viajaron en verano a Ucrania para recibir formación paramilitar. El PSOE justifica para personarse como acusación particular al amparo de la Ley de Enjuiciamiento Criminal que los investigados, “bajo una apariencia formal de asociación cultural y deportiva, pudieron haber constituido una estructura jerarquizada orientada a la promoción sistemática del odio, la discriminación y la violencia ideológica, con órganos directivos que aprueban y coordinan acciones de sus militantes, muchas de ellas violentas”. Núcleo Nacional surgió en las protestas contra el PSOE por la ley de amnistía en noviembre de 2023 y se define como “nacionalsocialista, antidemocrática y abiertamente antisemita”.

El PSOE hace hincapié en que se habrían llevado a cabo acciones delictivas a través del grupo ultra asturiano White Boys y después mediante concentraciones que derivaron en desórdenes públicos y agresiones a personas de ideología contraria en distintas ciudades españolas, “haciendo alusión en sus actuaciones a nuestro secretario general y presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez Pérez-Castejón, al PSOE y a su sede nacional en la calle Ferraz de Madrid, en diversas ocasiones a lo largo de estas”. Núcleo Nacional reclutaba nuevos miembros a través de White Boys, que realizaba “cacerías” humanas, fabricaba cócteles molotov e incluso portaba armas cortas de fuego, según el sumario del caso. “¿Por qué eres nazi?”, era una de las preguntas a los aspirantes a ingresar en la asociación extremista.

Núcleo Nacional también grabó a la Policía Nacional y organizaba “días de puños”, la forma en que denominaba a sus acciones violentas para reventar actos de activistas de izquierdas y en defensa de los inmigrantes o judíos. “Los hechos investigados, según lo conocido, podrían afectar a bienes jurídicos colectivos como la paz pública, la dignidad de la persona, la igualdad o el pluralismo político”, sostiene el PSOE. Ferraz señala que el Código Penal (artículo 510) “protege frente a conductas dirigidas contra grupos o personas por razones, entre otras, de ideología”. Y especifica que el artículo 515 establece como asociaciones ilícitas “las que tengan por objeto cometer algún delito o promuevan su comisión y las que fomenten, promuevan o inciten al odio, la hostilidad, la discriminación o la violencia contra personas, grupos o asociaciones por razón de su ideología”.

La organización ultra desmantelada es integrante de la alianza “Lucha Paneuropea por una Europa de Naciones”, formada por 15 entidades de distintos países como Honor et Patria y Semper Uniti (Rumania), Hussards Paris (Francia), Legión Húngara (Hungría), Der Dritte Weg (Alemania) o Prevrat (Croacia), Triangle Noir (Francia) y Propatria Hellas (Grecia), entre otras.

articles.preview: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv. "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic". They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
articles.body:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

- Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

- Published3 hours ago

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that - in the absence of any major success on the vast front line - the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles.title: Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
articles.summary: With crowds rallying behind El Salvador's deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.
articles.preview: With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer. The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.
articles.body:
With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.

The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.

Thousands turned out to cheer on the roughly 2,500 soldiers Bukele has sent since October. What began as a narrow mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians has grown into a much broader military operation.

For some of those who marched, the intervention is exactly what the country needs after years of kidnappings, killings, and displacement, with little sign of relief.

But even with the Haitian government’s backing and a warm reception from the public, questions are growing about what the troops are doing on the ground and what kind of mark Bukele will ultimately leave on Haiti.

Why are Salvadoran troops in Haiti?

The immediate trigger came on October 18, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) went missing after armed men attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince.

The force was created to help Haitian authorities deal with a security crisis that has grown more severe since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise. According to Reuters, gangs now control more than 80 percent of the capital region, with Haitian and international forces struggling to reclaim that territory.

Shortly after the technicians went missing, Bukele announced a new military operation in Haiti, sending 100 special forces soldiers to rescue them. Since then, he’s sent about 2,500 in total.

Most of them are operating outside the UN-backed force and outside the UN support office’s monitoring mechanisms, according to UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric.

And the deployment itself has turned from a narrow rescue operation to a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers joining Haitian security forces, the GSF, and private contractors, including Blackwater founder Erik Prince’s Vectus Global.

Bukele, who gained international notoriety for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that led to a sharp decline in crime but has drawn widespread condemnation over human rights abuses, has been aggressively promoting the deployment on social media.

He has posted dramatic videos of helicopter attacks on gang leaders’ properties and, more recently, footage of rallies cheering on his troops.

“I never expected anything like this,” he wrote in a Tuesday post accompanying a video of a rally. “I hear you loud and clear. I love you, too.”

Neither the Haitian government nor the Salvadoran government replied to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment about the troops in Haiti.

Why are some Haitians cheering on the Salvadoran troops?

The troops have landed amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti, with nearly 1.5 million people displaced from their homes, and violence making it difficult to access food and basic services. More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence, including security operations, since 2022, according to Reuters.

At rallies in Port-au-Prince and other parts of Haiti, demonstrators voiced support for the deployment. Some who spoke to The Associated Press news agency described losing loved ones to gang violence and being forced to leave their homes.

“The support we see from many Haitians comes from sheer desperation after years of failure and widespread terror,” Louimann Maceus, president of the human rights organisation Ensemble des Citoyens Competents a la Recherche de l’Egalite des Droits de l’Homme en Haiti (ECCREDHH), told Al Jazeera. “People are exhausted.”

“There is a genuine hope, especially among the hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people we work with who just want to return safely home,” said Maceus, who lives in Port-au-Prince.

That hope, he said, follows years of frustration with UN-backed forces, which he said had done little to improve security.

The Salvadoran deployment already outnumbers the GSF, according to numbers from the GSF’s special representative Jack Christofides, on October 18, when it had just surpassed 2,000 personnel.

International Crisis Group analyst Diego Da Rin also links some of the enthusiasm to what he describes as a really effective communication campaign by Bukele, whose videos of strikes on gang leaders’ homes are all over Haitian social media.

“These are symbolic wins that everybody was waiting for,” he said, adding that AI-generated videos were also circulating of gang leaders being arrested.

But support for the deployment is not universal. Da Rin pointed to the residents of gang-controlled areas.

“Many of these people, who clearly see the risks in these iron-fist operations, are extremely scared of being attacked and being collateral damage of any of these operations,” said Da Rin.

What have Salvadoran troops actually achieved?

Security force clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46 percent in the 21 days after the start of the deployment, compared to the 21 days before it, according to the conflict monitoring group the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).

ACLED estimated more than 100 people were killed in the same period, including at least 26 civilians.

Haiti’s Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier, however, said on Monday that the government had received no reports of civilian casualties in the latest operations, which it described as professional, according to Reuters.

Bukele has used social media to highlight what he sees as the offensive’s successes.

After Salvadoran troops joined Haitian police and a government task force in a November 8 attack on a house belonging to Wilson Joseph, leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang, Bukele posted video of helicopters repeatedly firing at the building, as people ran away from the area.

Joseph reportedly was not there and survived the attack.

A few days later, Haitian national police and Bukele announced that they’d retaken control of the national football stadium. Bukele shared video of robot dogs armed with rifles moving through the corridors of the stadium alongside troops, although it’s unclear how exactly they were used in the operation.

Da Rin said it was worth noting that police initially credited their officers and the task force with retaking the stadium before handing control over to Salvadoran troops, who set up a base there.

The stadium is a useful spot to launch operations against nearby gang strongholds, he added, but it represented a relatively small gain from positions Haitian forces had already secured.

On Wednesday, Bukele posted another video showing a helicopter attack on the home of Jeff Larose, leader of the Taliban gang, which controls the area of Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince.

It was not clear whether the attack had killed Larose or whether Haiti’s police or army had participated. The GSF was not involved, according to The Associated Press.

For displaced people looking to return home, the gains have yet to make a tangible difference, said Da Rin.

After the attack on Joseph’s house, none of the security forces set up a permanent presence in the area, he said.

“Armed groups were able to return and are now intimidating residents, searching their phones, threatening people suspected of sharing information with the security forces,” Da Rin told Al Jazeera.

He warned that forces appeared to be “in a race” to show results without a unified strategy to sustain them.

Salvadoran officials have said they plan to leave once the missing technicians are found. Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told the Associated Press earlier this month that they were dead, but their fate remains officially unknown.

“The priority should be to plan the most difficult part, how the forces will work together to establish lasting control,” said Da Rin.

Why are some experts concerned about the deployment?

The terms of the Salvadoran deployment haven’t been made public.

Amnesty International has called on both governments to explain who oversees the troops, what rules govern their use of force, and how civilians can safely report abuses.

On Monday, Salvadoran Vice President Felix Ulloa said the agreement would be kept under wraps until diplomatic conditions allowed its release and accused critics of having a “hidden agenda”.

Sam Vigersky, a fellow with the Council on Foreign Relations who studies emergency relief in response to armed conflict, said the lack of monitoring or publicly shared rules of engagement for Salvadoran troops operating outside the GSF means “we do not know what collateral damage might come of these offensives”.

For Vigersky, the lesson from past interventions, including a UN peacekeeping mission whose personnel brought cholera to Haiti and were implicated in widespread sexual abuse, is that “oversight matters”.

“Absent that,” he said, “the deep scars that Haiti has already from these past UN or other operations are only likely to grow.”

articles.summary: Presentata alla Knesset una proposta su limiti mandato e reati. Trump frena sull'attacco all'Iran
articles.preview: Netanyahu primo ministro per i prossimi due anni, in sincronia con il resto del mandato di Donald Trump, e dal 2028 presidente di Israele, quando a Gadi Eisenkot nell'accordo di rotazione toccherebbe la carica di premier. É la proposta su cui stanno lavorando alcuni esponenti politici israeliani e che dovrebbe essere presentata a Bibi e al leader del Change bloc. Il tema potrebbe essere discusso nell'incontro fissato per domenica tra i due gruppi.
articles.body:
Netanyahu primo ministro per i prossimi due anni, in sincronia con il resto del mandato di Donald Trump, e dal 2028 presidente di Israele, quando a Gadi Eisenkot nell'accordo di rotazione toccherebbe la carica di premier. É la proposta su cui stanno lavorando alcuni esponenti politici israeliani e che dovrebbe essere presentata a Bibi e al leader del Change bloc. Il tema potrebbe essere discusso nell'incontro fissato per domenica tra i due gruppi. Secondo le indiscrezioni ottenute da Ynet, Netanyahu non è disposto a rinunciare al ruolo di primo ministro in un eventuale governo di unità nazionale e insiste nel voler ricoprire il mandato per altri due anni.

Ma per l'alleanza del cambiamento ha parlato Yair Lapid, affermando che "sarebbe una follia e un rischio per Israele non rimuovere Netanyahu dall'incarico il prima possibile". E nel frattempo, il deputato di Yisrael Beytenu (il partito di Liberman) ha presentato a nome del Change bloc un disegno di legge che impone un limite di otto anni per il primo ministro e impedisce ai parlamentari incriminati per gravi reati penali di essere premier. In quest'ultimo caso, la proposta di legge prevede un meccanismo per la rimozione dall'incarico.

Netanyahu è sotto processo da sei anni per corruzione e frode. Il mandato del presidente Isaac Herzog terminerà il 7 luglio 2028. All'interno del Blocco del cambiamento si è creata una situazione complessa: ogni singolo leader di partito promuove un piano diverso e ostacola quelli dei partner.

Lieberman vuole stringere un'alleanza con gli ultrareligiosi, ma Natftali Bennett mette il veto. Eisenkot vuole un governo di minoranza, ma Lieberman e Bennett lo ostacolano. Bennett vuole l'unità, ma Lieberman, Eisenkot e Yair Golan non gradiscono. Emerge un disaccordo molto forte, che complica il lavoro di Eisenkot nel mettere insieme le tessere del puzzle e formare un nuovo governo.

Un'operazione militare per migliorare le possibilità di Netanyahu di rimanere in carica è stata adombrata dai media internazionali, con il Washington Post che cita fonti secondo cui il premier uscente avrebbe chiesto al capo del Mossad Roman Gofman di preparare un'operazione segreta contro l'Iran senza informare il gabinetto né il capo di stato maggiore dell'Idf, nel timore che possa opporsi ad un'operazione immediata.

Secondo Bloomberg, la probabilità che gli Stati Uniti lancino un'altra ondata di raid su larga scala contro la repubblica islamica è aumentata negli ultimi giorni, a causa degli attacchi dei Pasdaran e degli Houthi contro Riad (dove giovedi' e' stata danneggiata una torre che ospita la sede del fondo sovrano saudita nel distretto finanziario) e in Kuwait, e della situazione di stallo nei negoziati tra Usa e Teheran.

Fonti della sicurezza israeliana hanno riferito al sito di notizie Walla che qualora venisse dato il via libera dal presidente Trump all'azione militare contro il regime iraniano, all'escalation si unirebbe anche una coalizione militare dei Paesi del Golfo. L'obiettivo sarebbe quello di concentrare e abbreviare la durata della campagna puntando ai centri nevralgici del potere iraniano.

Dopo l'incontro di mercoledì a Tel Aviv con il capo dell'Idf Eyal Zamir e il direttore del Mossad, il comandante del Centcom Brad Cooper ha raggiunto l'Arabia Saudita per colloqui con alti funzionari nella capitale. Ma in una telefonata con l'emittente israeliana Channel 12 dal suo aereo di ritorno dal vertice in Cina con Xi Jinping e Vladimir Putin, Trump ha lasciato intendere che non ci sono attacchi imminenti: "Non ho fretta di prendere decisioni sull'Iran. Vedremo cosa succederà dopo l'inizio del nuovo anno".

articles.title: Senate Republicans in US reject measure to limit Trump’s war powers in Iran
articles.summary: The resolution was defeated 51-48. Three Republicans broke rank, voting against the measure.
articles.preview: The resolution was defeated 51-48. Three Republicans broke rank, voting for the measure. United States Senate Republicans have voted against a measure that would have required President Donald Trump to end the war on Iran or seek congressional approval to continue military action, reaffirming their support for the conflict despite recent electoral losses widely attributed in part to public opposition to the war. The resolution was defeated on Thursday 51 to 48. Senators voted largely along party lines.
articles.body:
The resolution was defeated 51-48. Three Republicans broke rank, voting for the measure.

United States Senate Republicans have voted against a measure that would have required President Donald Trump to end the war on Iran or seek congressional approval to continue military action, reaffirming their support for the conflict despite recent electoral losses widely attributed in part to public opposition to the war.

The resolution was defeated on Thursday 51 to 48. Senators voted largely along party lines. In September, the House of Representatives passed it 220 to 204.

The resolution, introduced under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, sought to direct Trump to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran.

Three Republicans – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky – voted with Democrats in favour of the measure. Only one Democrat, Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted against it. Fetterman has distanced himself from the Democratic Party and has expressed support for Israel and the war on Iran.

Thursday’s vote was the latest in a series of congressional attempts to curb Trump’s authority to order the US military into hostilities with Iran without authorisation from Congress. A similar measure passed the Senate in June, but subsequent efforts to restrict the president’s military authority failed. The resolution did not have the force of law and was largely symbolic.

Trump never sought congressional authorisation to wage war on Iran, although the US Constitution gives Congress the sole authority to declare war.

The vote also came amid mounting evidence of public dissatisfaction with the conflict. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published after the midterms found that 71 percent of Americans supported Congress passing legislation to end the war on Iran, including 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans.

A separate YouGov poll found that 44 percent of Americans were less likely to support candidates who backed the war, compared with 13 percent who were more likely to do so.

Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, a longtime advocate for restoring Congress’s constitutional authority over decisions to go to war, urged lawmakers to support the resolution. He argued that the election results reflected widespread dissatisfaction with the conflict and the rising cost of food, fuel and other goods.

“The unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election results of November 3,” Kaine said ahead of the vote.

articles.body:
Zimbabwe

The HALO Trust, the world's largest landmine clearance charity, reports that it has destroyed 250,000 landmines in Zimbabwe since 2013. This accomplishment marks a significant milestone in efforts to eliminate explosives left over from the liberation war of the 1970s.

The organization said its Zimbabwean teams have spent the past 13 years clearing minefields in the districts of Rushinga and Mount Darwin, helping restore farmland, reconnect communities and improve access to services. "We are super excited because again, it means a lot of things.

One, we're talking about peace of mind. Just that. It's one of the things that people often overlook, but then just knowing that this threat is gone and it is gone forever is just one of the biggest impacts of the work that we do of this mine being destroyed," said Nokutenda Masiyanise, Head of Donor Management and Partnerships at HALO Zimbabwe.

In Rushinga, HALO said clearance operations have benefited more than 14,000 residents by allowing families to graze livestock safely, cultivate crops, and access schools, clinics, markets, and water sources.

HALO, Zimbabwe’s largest demining operator, also employs local residents, including female deminers who often support large extended families.

The charity said it is using drones, advanced detectors and small excavators to speed up clearance efforts but warned that international aid cuts could jeopardize Zimbabwe’s goal of becoming mine-free by 2030.

articles.title: Dl scuola, gli e-book spaccano la maggioranza. FI vota contro, poi l'emendamento passa in Senato
articles.summary: AGI - L'avvertimento era arrivato ieri: Forza Italia è contraria alla norma sugli e-book . Ma FdI ha tenuto il punto sull'emendamento che stabilisce per gli editori l'obbligo di vendere la versione digitale dei libri scolastici e universitari a un prezzo inferiore di almeno il 50% rispetto alle edizioni cartacee. E così la maggioranza al Senato si spacca, con gli azzurri che votano contro e Azione che si aggiunge ai voti favorevoli delle altre forze di centrodestra. L'emendamento passa in Aula L'emendamento, presentato al Decreto Scuola, che tra le altre norme introduce il tetto del 30% di alunni stranieri con insufficiente conoscenza dell'italiano nelle classi, viene prima bocciato in Commissione Bilancio, sempre con i voti contrari di Forza Italia. Poi, messo in votazione in Aula, passa per 8 voti di differenza (84 sì e 76 no), con il via libera di FdI, presenti in massa, Lega e Noi Moderati, a cui si aggiungono i voti dei calendiani. Contrarie tutte le altre forze di opposizione, che protestano in Aula con cartelli e slogan. Il decreto, alla fine, viene approvato con i sì di tutto il centrodestra (80 voti favorevoli e 46 contrari) e trasmesso alla Camera per il via libera definitivo. Il peso delle assenze e il passaggio alla Camera 'Pesano' le assenze tra le fila delle opposizioni, che avrebbero potuto ribaltare l'esito del voto. Intanto nella maggioranza si guarda già all'iter a Montecitorio. Il decreto va convertito in legge entro il 29 novembre.
